The Forest dormouse Dryomys nitedula is a small glirid rodent inhabiting forest-steppe and montane woodlands from central Europe through the Caucasus and into central Asia. Neonates are exceptionally small, weighing just 1.73 grams [Wwb = 1.73 grams] at parturition, a birth mass that underscores their altricial developmental mode. This modest neonatal mass is comparable to that of other arboreal dormice and reflects the limited energetic reserves available to the gestating female. The species is viviparous, with embryos undergoing organogenesis and foetal development within the uterus. The tightly controlled thermal environment is critical for normal embryogenesis, as deviations can disrupt the delicate timing of foetal membrane development and placental nutrient transfer.

The cessation of lactation and the achievement of nutritional emancipation represent a critical developmental threshold, after which the growing young must forage independently in the arboreal environment. Delayed puberty is a common trait among hibernating glirids, as the annual cycle of torpor and arousal imposes significant physiological constraints on the timing of reproductive activation. Consequently, wild populations may exhibit even longer intervals to sexual maturation in years of poor autumn mast, when pre-hibernal fattening is curtailed.

Adult body mass in the Forest dormouse shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, with males generally attaining a larger ultimate wet weight. During the active season, individuals must accumulate sufficient lipid reserves to survive the prolonged winter hibernation, a period when all vital physiological functions are depressed. The relatively small body size of Dryomys nitedula compared to its sympatric congener Eliomys quercinus likely reflects dietary specialisation on softer mast items and arthropods, which impose different energetic constraints on growth.
